name: Chanterelle
colour: egg-yolk golden yellow throughout, cap and stem the same colour
mustRead: a funnel-shaped cap with a wavy, irregularly lobed margin
blunt forking ridges instead of gills, running down onto the stem
cap tapering smoothly into a solid stem, no ring
note: Commonly drawn with true blade gills and a flat cap; it has fat blunt forking ridges and a vase profile.

name: Morel
colour: tan to dark grey-brown pitted head, pale cream stalk
mustRead: a conical head of deep honeycomb pits with pale raised ridges
head fused to the stalk at its base, not sitting on it like a cap
hollow all the way through when halved
note: Not a wrinkled brain surface - the pits are recessed chambers with sharp ridge walls.

name: Black Truffle
colour: coal-black warty rind, purple-black flesh marbled with fine white veins
mustRead: an irregular lumpy nugget covered in small pyramidal warts
cut face marbled with a lace of white veins on dark flesh
no stem, no cap - it grows underground

name: Oyster Mushroom
colour: pale grey to fawn-brown cap, white gills and flesh
mustRead: fan or oyster-shell shaped caps in overlapping tiers on wood
white gills running all the way down to an off-centre stubby stem
a smooth, slightly inrolled wavy cap margin
note: Has real gills, unlike a true bracket - the stem is lateral or absent, never central.

name: Giant Puffball
colour: smooth chalk-white to buff, ageing olive-brown and cracked
mustRead: a huge featureless white ball sitting on the ground
leathery kid-glove skin with no cap, stem or gills
aged specimens split and puff a brown spore cloud

name: Bracket Fungus
colour: grey-brown zoned upper crust, pale cream pore surface beneath
mustRead: a hoof or half-disc jutting straight out of a tree trunk
concentric growth bands ridged across the top
a flat underside of fine pores, never gills
note: Distinguish from Shelf Fungus in this same set: a bracket reads as one thick woody hoof, the shelf as many thin tiers.

name: Stinkhorn
colour: white spongy stalk, dark olive-black slimy head
mustRead: a tall white pitted phallic stalk rising from a white egg sac
a thimble-shaped head coated in glistening olive-black slime
flies crawling on the slimy head

name: Earthstar
colour: leathery tan to grey-brown rays, paler grey spore sac
mustRead: a thick outer skin split into pointed rays peeled back like a star
a round papery spore sac sitting in the centre of the star
a single raised pore at the top of the sac

name: Fly Agaric
colour: scarlet cap with white warts, white stem and gills
mustRead: a domed scarlet cap studded with scattered white pyramid warts
a white pendulous ring skirt on the stem
a bulbous stem base ringed with scaly volval belts
note: The white flecks are loose veil scraps that wash off - they are not painted-on spots and should be irregularly spaced.

name: Death Cap
colour: olive-green to yellowish-green smooth cap, white gills and stem
mustRead: a smooth greenish cap with faint radiating fibrils, no warts
free white gills and a white skirt-like ring
a large sac-like white volva cupping the stem base
note: The bag-like volva at the base is the identifying feature and is usually omitted or buried in drawings.

name: Destroying Angel
colour: pure white all over, faintly ivory at the cap centre
mustRead: an entirely white mushroom, cap gills stem and all
a slender tall stem with a thin white ring
a sac-like white volval cup at the base

name: Shiitake
colour: umber to tea-brown cap, cream-white gills, tan fibrous stem
mustRead: a rounded brown cap with a cracked surface showing white flesh beneath
an inrolled cap margin fringed with white veil remnants
crowded white gills and a tough fibrous off-centre stem

name: Porcini
colour: chestnut to bun-brown cap, white to olive pore surface, pale buff stem
mustRead: a fat barrel or bulbous stem far thicker than the cap is tall
a spongy pore surface under the cap, absolutely no gills
a fine raised white net over the upper stem
note: Boletes are drawn with gills far too often - the underside must read as a sponge of tiny pores.

name: Lion’s Mane
colour: creamy white, yellowing to tan with age
mustRead: a rounded white pom-pom of long hanging icicle spines
spines all cascading downward from a single unbranched mass
no cap, no stem, no gills at all

name: Maitake
colour: grey-brown to fawn caps, white branching stalks and undersides
mustRead: a dense ruffled rosette of overlapping grey-brown spoon-shaped fronds
fronds all springing from a single branched white stalk base
the mass sitting like a hen at the foot of a tree

name: Enoki
colour: ivory white throughout when cultivated; tawny-orange sticky caps when wild
mustRead: a dense bundle of very long needle-thin stems fused at the base
tiny pinhead caps barely wider than the stems
the whole cluster reading as a bouquet, not a single mushroom
note: The supermarket white spindly form and the wild orange velvet-shanked form look nothing alike; pick one and commit.

name: Turkey Tail
colour: concentric bands of rust, ochre, blue-grey, cream and near-black; white pore underside
mustRead: thin flexible fan brackets banded in many contrasting concentric rings
a velvety surface with a pale cream wavy outer rim
dozens of small fans in overlapping rosettes along a log
note: The bands must vary in hue as well as tone - a single-colour ringed bracket reads as a different species.

name: Chicken-of-the-Woods
colour: brilliant sulphur-yellow to salmon-orange top, bright yellow pore underside
mustRead: thick fleshy overlapping shelves in vivid orange with yellow margins
a suede-soft wavy lobed edge
a bright yellow pore surface underneath

name: Cordyceps
colour: orange to ochre clubs, sometimes white; host insect dark brown
mustRead: slender clubs erupting directly out of a dead insect's body
the insect host still clearly recognisable beneath
a swollen roughened fertile head at the club tip
note: The insect must stay legible - without a visible host it is just a club fungus.

name: Bioluminescent Mushroom
colour: pale grey-cream by day, emitting a cold green-white glow in the dark
mustRead: small thin translucent caps clustered on rotting wood
a soft green light emitted from the gills and stem, not from the cap top
visible radial gill lines lit from within
note: The glow is a faint continuous green, not a bright yellow lamp; the light source is the gills.

name: Coral Fungus
colour: cream, ochre-yellow or salmon-pink, often with paler tips
mustRead: a dense upward-branching antler cluster from one thick base
branches dividing repeatedly into blunt or forked tips
no caps and no gills anywhere

name: Jelly Fungus
colour: translucent amber-orange to golden yellow, or brown when ear-shaped
mustRead: a wobbling gelatinous mass of convoluted brain-like folds
translucent enough that light passes through the lobes
sitting directly on bark with no stem

name: Shelf Fungus
colour: banded ochre and umber above, pale buff pore surface below
mustRead: several thin brackets stacked in overlapping tiers up a trunk
each shelf semicircular with a flat top and flat underside
the stack stepping outward like a staircase
note: Distinguish from Bracket Fungus in this same set: shelf reads as a tiered stack of thin plates, bracket as one thick solitary hoof.

name: Reindeer Lichen
colour: pale ash grey to grey-green, bleaching almost white when dry
mustRead: a spongy cushion of hollow tubular stalks branching in threes and fours
branch tips fine, drooping and all nodding one way
a springy mat texture with no leaves or flat lobes

name: Mold
colour: white fuzzy mat with blue-green, black or grey spore heads
mustRead: a low fuzz of tangled white hyphal threads
upright stalks each topped by a dark round spore capsule
colonies spreading in circular patches

name: Mildew
colour: chalky white to pale grey powder, greying-brown with age
mustRead: a flat powdery dusting sitting on a leaf or fabric surface
spreading as thin blotchy patches, not raised fuzz
the surface beneath still visible through the film
note: Mildew is superficial and powder-flat; drawing it as deep three-dimensional fluff makes it read as mold instead.

name: Yeast
colour: translucent pale cream to buff cells; beige paste in bulk
mustRead: rounded oval single cells with a smaller bud swelling off one side
bud scars pocking the cell wall
loose clusters of a few cells, never true filaments
note: Yeast is single-celled and has no hyphae, cap or stalk - it does not fit any macro-fungal body plan, so file it with the microscopic fungi.

name: Amoeba
colour: translucent colourless grey with a granular interior
mustRead: a shapeless blob throwing out blunt finger-like pseudopods
a clear outer rim around a granular grainy interior
one round nucleus and a clear circular contractile vacuole
note: The outline should be asymmetric and mid-flow - a neat symmetric star of arms reads as a heliozoan, not an amoeba.

name: Paramecium
colour: translucent pale grey-green, faintly straw tinted
mustRead: an asymmetric slipper or shoe outline, blunt at one end
the entire surface fringed with short beating cilia
a diagonal oral groove running into the cell side

name: Euglena
colour: grass green chloroplasts, translucent body, bright orange-red eyespot
mustRead: a spindle body, rounded at the front and drawn to a tail point
one long whipping flagellum from the front reservoir
a small red eyespot beside the flagellar base

name: Diatom
colour: glassy transparent silica shell, golden-brown chloroplasts inside
mustRead: a rigid glass shell built as two halves fitting like a pillbox and its lid
an intricate geometric lattice of pores, radial in discs or ribbed in boat shapes
clear silica through which the golden-brown plastids show
note: The pore pattern is precisely ordered and repeating, not random speckle - that regularity is the whole read.

name: Dinoflagellate
colour: amber to olive-brown armour, translucent at the edges
mustRead: a rigid armour of interlocking polygonal cellulose plates
a deep transverse groove belting the cell equator
two unequal flagella, one wrapped in the belt groove and one trailing behind
note: Many species carry long horns; the equatorial girdle groove is the non-negotiable feature.

name: Radiolarian
colour: clear glassy silica, faintly iridescent, with a dark central capsule
mustRead: a hollow sphere of glass built as an open geometric lattice
long fine straight spines radiating out from the shell
sometimes nested shells visible one inside another

name: Foraminiferan
colour: chalky white to honey-tan calcite shell
mustRead: a chambered shell coiling like a snail, each chamber larger than the last
shell walls pierced by fine pores
hair-thin branching pseudopodial threads streaming out from the aperture
note: The threads are fine, branching and net-forming, unlike an amoeba's fat blunt lobes.

name: Cyanobacteria
colour: blue-green to teal, some strains inky blue-black in mass
mustRead: beaded chains of identical cells strung end to end like a necklace
filaments curving and tangling into loose mats
occasional larger paler cells set into the chain

name: Methanogen
colour: pale grey-lilac, faintly translucent
mustRead: short blunt-ended rods clumped in irregular packets
gas bubbles rising away from the cluster
cells embedded in dark anoxic sediment or sludge
note: An archaean, not a bacterium - keep it plain and unflagellated, and let the escaping methane bubbles carry the identity.

name: Sulfur-Oxidizing Bacteria
colour: chalk-white filaments packed with bright lemon-yellow sulfur globules
mustRead: long unbranched white filaments lying in a tangled mat
each filament stuffed with refractile yellow sulfur granules
the mat sheeting over dark sediment or a vent surface

name: Iron-Oxidizing Bacteria
colour: rust orange to ochre-brown, cells themselves near-colourless
mustRead: a bean-shaped cell trailing a long twisted ribbon stalk behind it
the stalk crusted in rust-coloured iron oxide
stalks matting into an orange ochre sludge
note: The rust colour belongs to the secreted stalk, not to the cell body.

name: Nitrogen-Fixing Bacteria
colour: pale cream rods inside salmon-pink nodule tissue
mustRead: short rods packed densely inside a plant root nodule
swollen irregular Y-shaped bacteroid forms among the plain rods
the surrounding nodule flushed pink
note: The pink of an active nodule is leghaemoglobin in the host tissue and is a genuine identifying cue.

name: Halophile
colour: vivid magenta to carotenoid red-orange
mustRead: densely crowded rods staining the whole field hot pink
angular salt crystals scattered through the brine around them
some cells flattened into irregular squares or plates
note: The famous pink of salt ponds comes from the cells themselves - the brine should be tinted by their density, not dyed.

name: Thermophile
colour: warm yellow-orange to ochre, against pale mineral crust
mustRead: short thick-walled rods in dense streaming bands
banded orange mats following the outflow of hot water
steam and pale sinter mineral crust framing the colony

name: Acidophile
colour: colourless small rods in orange-red iron-stained acid water
mustRead: very small slender rods scattered in a rust-red fluid
orange iron precipitate flocking around the cells
corroded mineral grains and pyrite fragments nearby

name: Cryophile
colour: translucent blue-white, near colourless
mustRead: small rods trapped in thin liquid brine veins between ice crystals
faceted ice crystal boundaries framing the cells
a cold blue-white cast over the whole field

name: Radiation-Resistant Microbe
colour: salmon pink to red-orange, glossy
mustRead: spherical cells grouped as a flat packet of exactly four
an unusually thick layered cell envelope drawn as a heavy rim
a smooth pink-red glossy sheen
note: The tetrad grouping of four cocci is the signature - a lone sphere or a long chain reads as something else entirely.

name: Bioluminescent Plankton
colour: translucent pink-grey cells emitting cold electric blue light
mustRead: large near-spherical balloon cells, translucent and buoyant
a single stout trailing tentacle from a cleft in the cell
cold blue light sparking from the cells when the water is disturbed
note: The glow is blue-cyan, never green, and it flashes on agitation rather than shining continuously.

name: Red-Tide Algae
colour: brick red to rust brown, staining the surrounding water
mustRead: armoured plated cells with a girdle groove, packed at huge density
the water itself discoloured rust-red by the bloom
streaks and swirls of concentrated cells at the surface

name: Snow Algae
colour: deep crimson-red cysts, some still green-cored, on white snow
mustRead: thick-walled round resting cysts flooded with red pigment
a faint green chloroplast still showing at some cell centres
cells scattered through granular snow crystals, staining it watermelon pink

name: Tardigrade
colour: translucent amber-tan, gut contents showing darker green or brown
mustRead: a plump segmented barrel body with four pairs of stubby legs
each leg ending in a bunch of tiny curved claws
a blunt snout with a round tubular sucking mouth at the front
note: Eight legs, not six - the rearmost pair points backward and is used for gripping, not walking. It is a true animal, so give it real limbs rather than pseudopods.

name: Green Algae
colour: bright grass green with clear cell walls
mustRead: a hollow green sphere studded with many identical cells over its surface
smaller daughter colonies visible inside the parent sphere
clear jelly between the cells so the sphere reads as translucent
